summary: Redwood AE+SE ran an Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV caching and how those levers impact unit cost for Aurora Finance's conversational account-summary workload. Customer emphasized latency SLOs (<=200ms tail), strict PCI-related data controls, and desire to reduce token cost for high-throughput nightly jobs. Agreed to run a 1-week pilot to compare hosted vs dedicated with KV cache enabled; Redwood to send cost model and SOC2/VPC docs.
topics: Prefix vs KV cache behavior and hit rates
Cost model assumptions (tokens, GPU utilization, batching windows)
transcript:
Header: 2026-03-19 14:00 PDT | Duration: 46m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Raj Patel (Redwood SE), Leah Ortiz (Product), Sara Lopez (Aurora - Head of ML), Derek Wong (Aurora - Platform), Priya Iyer (Aurora - Security), Tom Baker (Aurora Eng Manager)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll kick off in a sec, um, just to confirm timezones — this is 14:00 PT for us, right?
[00:08] Sara Lopez: Yup, that's right, thanks Maya. We've been looking forward to this.
[00:12] Raj Patel: Cool, today is an Optimize walkthrough, we'll focus on batching and KV/prefix caching and run through a cost model for your account-summary use case. there may be a few slightly fuzzy transcriptions in the notes, apologies in advance.
[00:22] Derek Wong: Quick context: we're running a nightly job that summarizes customer ledger activity, heavy token counts, and then a chat-facing microservice that needs low tail latency under 200ms. we're trying to see where to put caching and if dedicated instances make sense.
[00:36] Maya Chen: Great. Sara, can you confirm current throughput and latency numbers?
[00:40] Sara Lopez: Yeah, throughput for the nightly batch is ~5 million tokens over a 2 hour window; chat requests average 6 rps with spikes to 60 during support peaks. tail p95 latency is around 320ms on our current setup.
[00:55] Raj Patel: ok that's helpful. so two workloads: high-throughput batch (cost-focused) and low-latency interactive (latency SLO). Our recommendations typically: use aggressive batching and quantization for the nightly job, and smaller batch windows + prefix/KV cache for chat to hit your 200ms p95.
[01:15] Tom Baker: when you say prefix cache vs KV cache, can you explain the difference again? sometimes our team's docs mix the terms.
[01:23] Raj Patel: Absolutely, quick high-level: prefix cache stores the beginning of an ongoing conversation — think cached encoder states and KV blobs for recent tokens so we avoid re-running the whole context. KV cache typically refers to keyed vector cache at token-level for reuse across requests (like repeated prompts, templates). in practice we implement both: prefix cache is more about per-conversation speed, KV cache helps hit rates when many requests share prefixes. sometimes we call it K-V cash in notes — sorry transcription issue.
[01:50] Leah Ortiz: Do you have typical hit-rate expectations for enterprise chat?
[01:54] Raj Patel: It varies; for templated flows we see 30-60% KV hit rates early on, and 70-90% for prefix cache on stable sessions depending on session length. for a banking chat where templates are common, i'd conservatively model 40-50% KV hits and 60% prefix hits.
[02:12] Sara Lopez: Great — if that aligns it could really cut tokens. What's the tradeoff on memory / GPU footprint?
[02:18] Raj Patel: Memory grows linearly with cache entries; with our Dedicated configs you can allocate node-local cache with eviction policies. the cost is RAM and some CPU for cache management; we modeled a mid-size pool for your pilot — it'll be cheaper in net tokens but you'll need nodes with slightly larger memory.
[02:34] Derek Wong: We're also strict on data residency and PCI; we need KMS integration and audit logs. is that part of the Dedicated offering?
[02:42] Maya Chen: Yes — Private/Dedicated supports customer KMS and audit logs. we'll attach SOC2 docs and the VPC architecture diagram in the follow-up.
[02:49] Priya Iyer: For audit: do you have per-token tracing or just request-level logs?
[02:54] Raj Patel: We provide request-level logs, token cost breakdowns and per-route tracing. we can enable extended observability for compliance (longer retention) as an add-on.
[03:05] Maya Chen: Ok jumping into the cost model slide... (screen share) our cost model separates three levers: batching window size, cache hit rate, and model variant/quantization.
[03:18] Raj Patel: Example: for a 32-token average response, at 50% KV hit rate and batching window of 30ms we see a 35% cost reduction versus no cache and small batches. but note that increasing batching window reduces tail latency when concurrent load is low, but can push p95 over your 200ms SLO in interactive flows.
[03:39] Tom Baker: do you support dynamic batching policies? like low-latency requests bypass the big batcher?
[03:44] Raj Patel: Yes — smart routing lets you pin routes to low-latency pools, or set policy to route priority traffic to nodes with batch window = 0. we demoed fallback rules in the console earlier.
[03:55] Sara Lopez: For the nightly job, what's the recommendation on quantization? we've been hearing about 8-bit and 4-bit tradeoffs.
[04:02] Raj Patel: Nightly batch is a great candidate for aggressive quantization (4-bit) if it tolerates minor accuracy drift. we'll run evals on your prompt set to validate. Quantization reduces memory and increases throughput so the cost per token drops significantly.
[04:17] Derek Wong: Any caveats re: hallucinations with lower precision?
[04:20] Raj Patel: It's model-dependent; our Optimize tool flags quality regressions on your eval set; we'll include a baseline comparison. for financial summarization, we typically keep a conservative quantization profile and have guardrails for factuality checks.
[04:33] Maya Chen: here's a quick worked example in the spreadsheet: assume 100k chat tokens/day, 50% KV hit-rate, 60% prefix hit-rate for returning sessions; with batching we reduce GPU utilization by 20% and tokens billed by ~40%, net savings ~37% after factoring node cost.
[04:52] Sara Lopez: That's compelling. Could you run that example with our real numbers? we can share sample logs.
[04:56] Maya Chen: Absolutely; Raj will outline the pilot measurement plan.
[05:00] Raj Patel: Pilot plan: 1) baseline capture (1 day) of current traffic; 2) enable KV/prefix cache on a test route for 1 week with telemetry; 3) compare cost and latency, and run the eval suite daily. We'll need access to anonymized logs and a small test cluster/VPN.
[05:18] Derek Wong: VPN + test cluster — ok we can provision. who do we share access with?
[05:22] Maya Chen: Send it to pilot-aurora@redwood.ai or directly to me and raj; we'll coordinate.
[05:27] Priya Iyer: Security question: are cached items encrypted at rest and in transit?
[05:32] Raj Patel: Yes — cache and KV blobs are encrypted at rest using customer-managed KMS for Dedicated/Private; in transit TLS. We'll send the KMS integration doc.
[05:42] Tom Baker: About metrics — can the console show hit rates and per-route cost in near real time?
[05:47] Leah Ortiz: Yes, console shows token-level cost, hit rates, per-route latency percentiles, and we can add annotations for rollout changes.
[05:55] Sara Lopez: Ok, objections from our infra team: if we go Dedicated, there's an ops overhead. what's the team size needed?
[06:01] Maya Chen: Dedicated is managed; Redwood handles runtime and upgrades. you'll need one infra engineer to handle networking/K8s side for private deploys, but for Redwood-managed Dedicated we take most of the ops work.
[06:13] Derek Wong: That helps. Pricing question: how do you price caching? like extra for cache memory?
[06:18] Maya Chen: Primary cost drivers are compute and model variant. cache memory is included in node sizing; we show it in the cost model as slight incremental node cost. pricing is committed capacity + per-token for hosted; Dedicated is reserved nodes with a predictable monthly fee. We'll send pricing scenarios against the pilot numbers.
[06:34] Raj Patel: One more nuance: cold cache vs warm cache. initial pilot days might show lower hit rates; model the first 48 hours as cold and then steady state. We recommended running the pilot 7 days to capture both behaviors.
[06:49] Sara Lopez: Makes sense. Any potential gotchas with prefix caching for long conversations?
[06:54] Raj Patel: Eviction policy: we keep recent prefixes and evict by LRU or TTL; very long sessions might not fully benefit, but most banking sessions are short so prefix hit remains high.
[07:06] Tom Baker: For the pilot, what's success criteria?
[07:09] Maya Chen: We suggested three success criteria: 1) p95 latency <= 200ms on interactive route, 2) >=30% reduction in token billing for batch+chat combined, 3) no quality regressions on the eval suite (pass rate >=95%).
[07:23] Priya Iyer: We'll want the SOC2 and detailed audit scope before signing pilot SOW.
[07:28] Maya Chen: Understood — we'll attach SOC2 package and the VPC diagram in the follow-up email.
[07:33] Raj Patel: Quick demo clip — console shows we can flip caching per-route and roll back if latency increases. (small pause)
[07:45] Sara Lopez: Nice. can you also show the per-token cost delta for quantization?
[07:49] Raj Patel: Sure on the spreadsheet — 8-bit reduces cost by ~20% vs FP16, and 4-bit can be ~40-55% depending on kernel and model. we'll run model-specific numbers for your prompts.
[08:05] Tom Baker: any competitor features we should watch for? like Anthropic's response latency claims?
[08:09] Raj Patel: Competitors have different tradeoffs; some restrict model variants, some don't offer the same caching primitives or private deployment flexibility. We'll include a short competitor matrix in the follow-up.
[08:20] Maya Chen: Ok wrapping up — recap: Redwood will send cost-model spreadsheet, SOC2 and VPC/KMS docs, and schedule pilot setup for next Wed 03/25. Aurora to provision VPN/test cluster and anonymized sample logs.
[08:35] Sara Lopez: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[08:38] Derek Wong: Thanks.
[08:40] Maya Chen: Thanks, talk soon.

Notes: occasional transcription errors (K-V cash, n-gram -> nvgram), speaker labels sometimes generic. References shared: link to cost-model spreadsheet (https://redwood.ai/sheets/aurora-cost-model), VPC diagram (doc link), SOC2 package (doc link).
